strengths: They use a new architecture to model protein data.
They have many different sources of validation which have the potential to be convincing.
The method is novel and explores a region of algorithm space that is generally underexplored for proteins, namely sequence-based design and in particular MSA-based design.
Results are competitive if not necessarily state of the art. I consider the paper more about new ideas and approaches as opposed to necessarily achieving the best results.
The method essentially finds a niche between quality and novelty of generated structures, sitting in between existing methods on the Pareto frontier.
Experiments are well done and the algorithm itself appears clever.
The results are overall quite impressive, achieving state-of-the-art results in some measurements while still attaining decent performance in metrics where it is outperformed.
The use of Bayesian Flow Networks, which are not mainstream in protein modeling, provides a high degree of novelty.
The introduction to Bayesian Flow Networks in Section 2.2 greatly improves readability.
The paper emphasizes mathematical derivation and provides clear explanations of key theoretical components.
The authors benchmark ProfileBFN against multiple state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating performance on par with or surpassing existing approaches.
weaknesses: The introduction should be written more carefully, especially regarding de novo design and its role in library design versus directed evolution.
The claim that the method tends to produce proteins too similar to the original wild type is not backed up by empirical data in the literature.

It makes little sense to position their "protein family design" as a third way; the paragraph should compare their method with PoET and EvoDiff and put it in context in a library → optimization pipeline.
The related works section has a similar issue.
The paper understates prior methods that have modeled protein families, such as PoET and ProtMamba, which should be clearly mentioned in the introduction and related works.
The authors should provide an argument for why their method is expected to outperform those prior methods despite not training on protein family data.
The introduction of the model is too colloquial; it should describe Bayesian Flow Networks with proper generative process and likelihood terminology (e.g., explain VLB).

The claim of offering a more efficient and practical solution by bypassing the need to construct an MSA profile training set is framed from the authors' perspective rather than practitioners', and the authors should simply curate a training dataset as other developers have done.
Important evaluation details, including definitions of metrics and how enzymatic activity is predicted, are relegated to the appendix instead of the main text.

The evaluation focuses on diversity and novelty rather than sampling more sequences from the conditioned protein family, which is the proper goal; these statistics should be compared to those of the real family.
How the evaluations are precisely done is not well described at all.
The mathematics is not presented in an easy-to-understand way for the reader.
Reuse of variable names is an issue.
In line 170, dimensions are given for the summation symbol, which is nonsensical because summation is an operator, not a data type.
Explanations for many of the results feel rushed, requiring the reader to put a lot of effort into parsing them.
The paper lacks some depth in application despite its strength on the mathematical side.
